[spoiler]From the air, Western View still looked like a paradise. A green jewel in the endless blue of the Nestor Ocean, its coastline was wrapped in white sand and ringed with harbors. But that was the postcard view.
On the ground, the truth was harder to romanticize. Wessernia, the capital, stretched for miles in every direction, its skyline a thicket of high-rises that seemed to press inward on themselves. Streets were jammed with traffic, construction cranes loomed over every neighborhood, and the sidewalks pulsed with a human tide.
The numbers were blunt: the island could comfortably sustain sixty-two million people. It now holds over one hundred million.
The price of imported food had tripled in a decade. Timber imports were at record highs because domestic forests had been stripped bare. Iron and bauxite were gone. The fishing industry had collapsed under decades of overharvesting.
And so, in the glass-and-steel heart of Wessernias Government Complex, the Council of Thirteen gathered to decide the nations future.
The council chamber was a semi-circular room with tiered seating. Digital screens along the walls streamed live news coverage and resource data.
At the center, seated at the head of the curve, was Mack Messiaon. In his early sixties, with a neatly trimmed beard and a habit of speaking in short, precise sentences, he was a man who had risen through politics by rarely wasting words.
This, he said, tapping the display embedded in his desk, is where our future lies.
On the wall behind him, the map of the Nestor Ocean shrank, and the eastern continent of Armaralo filled the screen.
Satellite imagery revealed sprawling forests, winding rivers, deepwater ports, and mineral-rich mountain belts. Small city clusters gleamed along the coastlines. It was not empty  far from it  but vast enough to dwarf Western View a hundred times over.
Weve known this for years, said Councilor Iren Solvek, a pragmatic figure from the islands industrial south. What we havent done is decide what were willing to risk to get it.
Councilor Mara Den, the youngest on the council, leaned forward. We cant keep throwing bandages on a wound thats bleeding out. In twenty years, well be looking at population collapse. The only responsible move is to start an expansion program now.
Expansion, scoffed Councilor Varrin Kehl from the agricultural districts. Thats a polite way of saying were planning to land people on another sovereign landmass and start taking space.
Messiaon held up a hand before the argument could sharpen. We will not go in blind. We will not go hostile. But we will go. The alternative is staying here and watching our nation choke.
Councilor Halrik, whose district had suffered some of the worst resource shortages, asked the question no one wanted to say aloud:
And if Armaralos governments say no?
Messiaons gaze was steady. Then we will negotiate until we can find one that says yes.
The council chamber fell silent.
Messiaon let the pause stretch, then said, I will put it to a vote. Approval for the Armaralo Initiative  a multi-phase program to establish a Wessern presence on the continent. Phase One: reconnaissance, diplomacy, and logistics assessment. Phase Two: settlement.
The chamber hummed with quiet tension as Councilor Solvek called the roll. Each council members vote would chart the fate of a nation on the brink.
One by one, the thirteen hands rose or stayed down.
Councilor Solvek?
Approve.
Councilor Den?
Approve.
Councilor Kehl?
Oppose.
The tally was close, but when the final vote was counted, the Armaralo Initiative passed with eight in favor and five opposed.
Mack Messiaon allowed himself a rare, brief smile. Thank you, councilors. This is the first step toward securing Western Views future.
Within days, the government announced the formation of the Vanguard Task Force  a team of experts and envoys tasked with conducting thorough reconnaissance on Armaralo. The team included diplomats, scientists, engineers, linguists, and security personnel equipped with the latest satellite uplinks, drones, and advanced surveying technology.
Head Council Messiaon personally oversaw the selection process. Among those chosen was Captain Lira Taven, a seasoned operations leader with years of experience in complex multinational missions, and Dr. Eshan Riya, a cultural anthropologist specializing in intercontinental relations.
On a brisk morning at Wessernia International Port, the Vanguards flagship, the MV Horizon, readied for departure. Its hull gleamed under the rising sun, packed with modular habitat units, scientific instruments, vehicles, and communication arrays.
As the ship slipped into the vast Nestor Ocean, the weight of history pressed on every soul aboard.

Back on the island, the people watched with a mix of hope, pride, and apprehension. Media outlets buzzed with debates, and neighborhoods held forums discussing the potential impact of expanding into Armaralo  a continent rich in resources but also home to established nations and cultures.
After a two-week voyage across the Nestor Ocean, the MV Horizon approached the eastern coast of Armaralo. The ships advanced sensors and drones relayed images of the shoreline: dense forests gave way to sprawling settlements interwoven with roads, ports bustling with cargo ships, and farmlands stretching inland.
Captain Lira Taven stood on the bridge, eyes scanning the horizon. Were not stepping onto unclaimed land, she said, voice steady but tinged with caution. This is a continent with people  governments, communities, histories.
Dr. Eshan Riya nodded. Thats why diplomacy will be crucial. Were here as guests, not invaders.

The Vanguard team established a temporary base near a coastal city named Valmira, where local officials had been cautiously informed of their arrival through diplomatic channels. The citys architecture was a blend of modern high-rises and historic stone buildings, vibrant markets, and cultural diversity reflecting Armaralos complex history.
Meetings with Armaralo government representatives began in a sleek municipal building overlooking the harbor. The discussions were polite but firm. The Armaralans emphasized their sovereignty and expressed concerns over resource competition and cultural impact.

Despite the challenges, both sides saw opportunities. The Wesserns proposed joint scientific research, technology exchange, and trade partnerships, emphasizing that Western Views overcrowding made cooperation a necessity rather than conquest.
Meanwhile, on the island of Western View, news of the negotiations stirred hope and unrest. Pro-expansion advocates praised the efforts as vital, while skeptics warned of potential conflicts and cultural erasure.
The sleek conference room overlooking Valmiras harbor became the arena for intense discussions. Thirteen delegates from Armaralos coastal regions sat opposite the Wessern Vanguard team, mirroring the thirteen council members back home in Wessernia.
Head Council Messiaons envoy, Councilor Reva Dorn, led the Wessern delegation with measured diplomacy. She laid out the Armaralo Initiative: a phased expansion prioritizing sustainability, cultural respect, and resource sharing.

Armaralos chief negotiator, Minister Kaelen Vash, was firm. Our lands and resources belong to the people of Armaralo. Any agreement must respect our sovereignty and ensure our communities benefit, not suffer.
Councilor Dorn nodded. We agree. We propose joint oversight committees, shared development projects, and protection of cultural sites. Western View seeks not to displace but to coexist.

Meanwhile, back on Western View, public opinion was fracturing. News outlets covered peaceful demonstrations alongside protests warning against imperial ambitions. Food shortages worsened, increasing pressure on the council to act swiftly.

Scientific surveys conducted by the Vanguard revealed vast mineral deposits inland, fertile soils, and significant freshwater sources  exactly the resources Western View needed to rebuild its industries and sustain its growing population.
Yet, as the Wesserns planned their first settlement near Valmira, whispers of unrest spread through Armaralos hinterlands. Some locals saw the newcomers as an opportunity, others as a threat.
The area designated for Western Views first settlementofficially named New Wessernialay on a gentle coastal plain just outside Valmira. Construction began in earnest as prefabricated housing modules, machinery, and supplies were unloaded from the MV Horizon and its support vessels.
Heavy equipment carved out roads, erected power grids, and laid the groundwork for water treatment facilities. Teams of engineers and scientists worked alongside local contractors, signaling a commitment to partnership.

For many locals, the settlement brought jobs and fresh economic opportunities. Fishermen sold fresh catch to Wessernian cooks, artisans traded handcrafted goods for modern tools, and clinics set up by Wesserns provided much-needed medical services.
Councilor Reva Dorn frequently hosted town hall meetings, encouraging dialogue between settlers and local leaders. At first, the atmosphere was cautiously optimistic.

But beneath the surface, fault lines began to appear.
Some Armaralans resented the rapid pace of Wessernias growth, worrying that their lands and resources might soon be overwhelmed. Rumors circulated that Wessern settlers were staking claims far beyond the agreed boundaries.
On Western Views side, impatience grew. Reports of supply shortages back home intensified calls within the Council to accelerate expansion  voices advocating for more settlers, faster resource extraction, and greater military presence to protect Wessern interests.

One evening, Jaren Korr, a young Wessern engineer assigned to infrastructure projects in New Wessernia, overheard a heated conversation between local farmers and a group of Wessern foresters.
They are cutting deeper into the forests than promised, one farmer said, eyes narrowed. Our sacred groves are being destroyed.
A Wessern forester replied sharply, Were clearing only whats necessary. Our people need timber and land. If the locals cant see that, they dont understand our survival.

The delicate balance of cooperation was fraying. Back in Wessernia, Head Council Messiaon convened emergency sessions with the Council of Thirteen, grappling with how to manage both the expansions promise and its perils.
As the months passed, the initial goodwill between the Wessern settlers and Armaralos locals began to erode. Reports filtered back to Wessernia of protests near New Wessernia  gatherings of Armaralan villagers demanding respect for their land and rights.
One such protest turned violent when a group of settlers clashed with demonstrators trying to block a logging operation near the sacred groves. No lives were lost, but several were injured, and the incident made headlines across both continents.

In the Council chamber in Wessernia, Head Council Mack Messiaon called an emergency session. The room was tense, voices raised as councilors debated the way forward.
Councilor Varrin Kehl, long skeptical of the expansion, said bluntly, Weve brought conflict to their shores and instability to our own people. This isnt just about resources anymoreits about sovereignty and respect. We must slow the expansion, or risk losing everything.
Councilor Mara Den, ever the optimist, countered, We cant stop now. Our people are desperate. We need stronger enforcement, better diplomacy, and a clear strategy to stabilize New Wessernia.
Messiaon listened carefully, then addressed the chamber. We face a crossroads. Either we redouble our efforts to peacefully integrate with Armaralos communities, or we prepare for a longer, more difficult struggle.

Meanwhile, Armaralos regional government increased patrols near the settlement and deployed diplomats to negotiate protections for their citizens. Secret talks hinted at the formation of local resistance groups wary of Wessern influence.

Back in New Wessernia, Councilor Reva Dorn organized cultural exchange programs and joint environmental committees, striving to mend fences. Yet, she knew these were stopgap measures against a tide of growing mistrust.
Tensions in New Wessernia reached a boiling point one rainy evening when a construction crew, backed by Wessern security personnel, attempted to expand a road through territory claimed by a local Armaralan village.
Despite warnings, the crew proceeded, triggering a confrontation. Villagers erected barricades and confronted the workers. The situation escalated rapidly when a scuffle broke out, and shots were fired  not by the locals, but by a panicked Wessern security guard.

The incident left two Armaralan villagers wounded and ignited outrage across the continent. News spread quickly, sparking protests in Valmira and calls from Armaralos government for an immediate halt to Wessern expansion.
Western Views media exploded with conflicting narratives  some portraying the villagers as aggressors, others condemning the security teams use of force.

In Wessernia, the Council of Thirteen convened in crisis. Messiaon, visibly worn but resolute, addressed the chamber.
We cannot allow this incident to spiral into full conflict. Our people need to understand that expansion carries risks  but we must also stand firm in securing our future.
Councilor Kehl demanded, Then we must review our presence there immediately. Increase transparency. If necessary, withdraw until real agreements are made.
Councilor Den opposed, Withdrawal is surrender. We must increase support to New Wessernia, both diplomatic and security.

International mediators arrived from neighboring Armaralan nations, urging both sides to de-escalate. Backchannel negotiations commenced, seeking a roadmap to peace.

Meanwhile, grassroots movements formed on both sides  Armaralan groups demanding sovereignty and protection, and Wessern settlers advocating for their right to a new home.
Months of tense diplomacy followed the shooting incident. International mediators facilitated meetings between Western Views Council delegates and Armaralos government officials. The world watched closely, fearing a wider conflict that could destabilize the entire region.

Councilor Reva Dorn emerged as a pivotal figure, tirelessly advocating for a peaceful resolution. In private talks with Armaralos lead negotiator, Minister Kaelen Vash, she acknowledged the deep wounds the expansion had caused but stressed the dire needs driving Western View.

After long discussions, a compromise began to take shape:

Western View would be allowed to continue establishing settlements on Armaralo under strict territorial limits.

All expansion would require prior approval from Armaralo authorities, ensuring no unauthorized land grabs.

Wessern settlements would operate autonomously without integration or reliance on local Armaralan communities  meaning no employment, no resource sharing, and no joint infrastructure.

Armaralo would retain sovereignty and control over its people and resources outside of the Wessern areas.

Both sides would establish a joint monitoring commission to oversee compliance and mediate disputes.

The agreement, though far from ideal for either side, was presented publicly as a pragmatic solution to an unavoidable reality. Western View secured the land it desperately needed, while Armaralo maintained formal control and limited exposure to Wessern influence.

Back in New Wessernia, the mood was cautious but hopeful. Expansion projects resumed with renewed focus on self-sufficiency. Wessern engineers and workers increased efforts to develop independent agriculture, energy, and manufacturing systems.

Councilor Dorn addressed the settlers: This is not the future we dreamed of  its a compromise. We must build a home here, on our own terms, and respect the boundaries set for us.

Meanwhile, on Armaralo, many locals continued to watch the Wessern settlements warily, aware that the uneasy truce was fragile. But for now, the guns were silent, and both sides looked toward a tense peace.
But not every settler came with the same boring old story, in fact here are just a few of the many stories Armarlo made. Jalen Meris was just eight years old when he boarded the Sea Promise, one of the many ships carrying Wessern settlers bound for Armaralo. His parents, engineers assigned to critical infrastructure projects, had been placed on a different vessel due to the governments strict capacity rules.
The last moments at the Wessernia port were a blur of hugs and tears. Be brave, Jalen, his mother whispered as the ships horn blew. Well see you soon.

The Sea Of Promise was filled with a mix of families, workers, and officials. For Jalen, the voyage was both terrifying and exciting. The endless ocean stretched beyond sight, and the hum of the ships engines never ceased.
Within days, Jalen found himself feeling lonely and out of place. His parents absence weighed heavily on him. But aboard the ship, he discovered others just like him  children of settlers, each with their own stories of separation and hope.

One of them was Mara, a spirited girl a year older, who quickly took Jalen under her wing. She introduced him to the other children, teaching him games that helped them pass long hours on the deck.
The group formed their own little community, sharing snacks, stories, and dreams of the new land waiting for them.

As the Sea Promise neared Armaralo, Jalens anxiety returned. Would his parents be there when he arrived? Would the new land be a home or a strange, cold place?
The day they docked, Jalen ran through the bustling port of New Wessernia, clutching a small toy his mother had given him  a carved wooden bird  a reminder that family ties endured across distance.

Once ashore, Jalen began school with other settler children. He struggled at first, missing his parents and adjusting to the unfamiliar environment, but his new friends helped him find his place.
Through their laughter and shared adventures, Jalen started to believe that maybe, just maybe, this new land could become home.
Years later, a much taller, more confident Jalen stood on the edge of a bustling New Wessernia plaza. His parents, who had returned months earlier after finishing their assignments, hugged him tightly.
Look how much youve grown, his mother smiled.
Jalen grinned. Ive made friends here. This is home now.

Elda Tavan sat quietly in the wooden rocking chair by her window, the late afternoon sun casting long shadows over the worn floorboards of her small home in Wessernias Old Quarter. Outside, the city hummed with the noise of progress  construction cranes scraping the sky, the distant rumble of traffic, and the ever-present murmur of hundreds of thousands of lives pressed tightly together on their crowded island.
At eighty-two years old, Elda had seen Western View change in ways she never imagined. She remembered when the island had been a place of space and quietfamilies tending small gardens, children running freely across fields, neighbors gathering in open-air markets. Now, those fields were gone, replaced by endless rows of apartments and high-rises that swallowed the sunlight.
The decision to expand eastwardto send their people across the Nestor Ocean to Armaralowas a subject that filled her with both hope and unease. Hope, because the island was choking under the weight of too many people and too few resources. Unease, because she feared what might be lost in the process.
Her grandson, Jalen, was among those chosen to leave. A boy of only eight, full of curiosity and boundless energy. Elda had spent long nights crafting letters to send with the first waves of settlers, letters filled with stories of their home: the songs sung at festivals, the recipes handed down from their ancestors, the lessons learned from hard times and triumphs alike.

Eldas trembling hand traced the lines of an old photograph she kept in her lap  a family portrait taken decades ago beneath the blooming jacaranda tree that had since been cut down to make way for a new road.
She wondered if Jalen understood what it meant to carry their culture so far from home, to become a seed planted in foreign soil.

In the small community center, Elda had taken to gathering with other elders, their voices soft but resolute. They spoke of traditions, of language, and of the importance of passing their identity to the next generation.
We cannot let the hunger for land swallow who we are, Elda told them, her voice steady despite the weight of years. Our stories, our songs, our history  they are the roots that keep us strong.
Yet, she also recognized that survival demanded change. The islands limits were real. The decision to expand was no longer a matter of choice but of necessity.

One evening, as dusk settled, Elda sat down to write another letter to Jalen. She told him of the jacaranda blossoms, of the markets where she once bargained for spices, and of the stars that shone over Wessernias harbor.
Remember who you are, she wrote, and carry our home with you  not just in your heart but in your actions. Be kind, be brave, and never forget that we are one people, no matter where we stand.

Elda folded the letter carefully and placed it with the others in a small wooden box. She knew that the world was changing fast, and that her role was to be the keeper of memory and the voice of calm in a storm of uncertainty.
As night deepened, she listened to the distant sounds of the city  the hum of progress and the heartbeat of a nation searching for its future.

Ravi Koothar wiped the sweat from his brow as he surveyed the dusty construction site just outside New Wessernias growing perimeter. The late morning sun beat down mercilessly, reflecting off the pale sand that stretched to meet the dense forests of Armaralo beyond.
The task before him was daunting: design and oversee the construction of the settlements water treatment system. It was the lifeblood of the new city, the key to making this foreign land a home for thousands of Wessern settlers who depended on safe, reliable water.

Back on the island of Western View, Ravi had been a well-respected civil engineer working on urban infrastructure projects. But nothing had prepared him for the complexities of building a modern city almost from scratch, thousands of miles away  on a land unfamiliar in every way.

From day one, the challenges piled up.
The local soil, different from the islands volcanic base, demanded new foundation techniques. The heavy rains typical of Armaralos climate threatened to flood construction zones. Equipment shipments arrived late or incomplete due to strained logistics.
Most difficult, perhaps, was navigating the cultural divide.
While many Armaralan workers were hired to help with physical labor, trust was slow to build. Some locals were wary of Wessern intentions, cautious about the rapid changes happening on land their ancestors had stewarded for centuries.
Ravi found himself in more meetings than he ever expected  not just with his engineering teams, but with community leaders, local supervisors, and occasionally the Armaralan liaison officers.

One afternoon, Ravi sat down with a small group of local workers after a long day. They shared stories in broken English and the closest Armaralan dialect he could manage. Over steaming cups of strong tea, he learned about their traditions and hopes for the future.
In those moments, Ravi realized that the success of his project hinged not only on technical skill but on human connection.

Despite setbacks  a delayed pump shipment here, an unexpected underground water source discovered there  Ravis water treatment plant slowly began to take shape.
It was more than a building. It was a symbol: the fragile promise of coexistence, a foundation for survival in a new world.

Each evening, exhausted but determined, Ravi returned to his small quarters in New Wessernia. He sketched new designs by the light of a single bulb, thinking of the thousands who would drink clean water thanks to his work.
And he wondered what kind of city they were building  one that could endure not just the climate and geography, but the complicated human stories unfolding beneath its surface.

Lina Vash stood at the front of her classroom in a modest schoolhouse just beyond the city of Valmira, the coastal hub closest to the expanding Wessern settlement. Outside, the sounds of the bustling harbor mingled with distant hums of machinery from New Wessernia.
Her students were a mix of local Armaralan childrencurious, bright-eyed, and full of questions about the changes reshaping their world. Many asked about the Wesserns: Who were they? Why were they here? Would they stay forever?

Linas own feelings were conflicted. She was proud of her heritage, deeply connected to the land and its history. The arrival of thousands of settlers from Western View had brought both promise and fear to her community.
In the early days, some families had welcomed opportunities for trade and work. Others viewed the newcomers as invaders, fearing the loss of their land and culture.

Determined to bridge the growing divide, Lina organized community forums and cultural exchange workshops. She invited elders to share stories of Armaralos past and encouraged her students to learn the Wessern language alongside their native tongue.
At times, the work was exhausting. Some meetings ended in heated arguments; others in silence heavy with unspoken mistrust.

One afternoon, after a particularly tense community gathering, Lina sat quietly with a small group of children. She told them a story passed down through generationsa tale of two rivers converging to create a stronger current, rather than clashing and eroding each other.
Change is hard, she said softly. But if we learn to flow together, perhaps we can build something better for everyone.

Linas hope was cautious but real. She believed education could plant seeds of understanding, preparing her students to live in a world where their homeland was no longer alone, but part of a larger, more complex community.

As the sun set over Valmira, Lina packed her books and looked toward the lights of New Wessernia in the distance. The future was uncertain, but she was determined to help her people navigate it with wisdom and compassion.

The rugged Pantgruel Mountains, towering like ancient sentinels along the Pantgruel-Shamat Fault Line, had long been revered for their breathtaking beauty and untamed wilderness. When the Council of Thirteen approved the expansion into this region of Armaralo, the vision was clear: a world-class ski resort and mountain city that would bring prestige and tourism revenue to Western View.
New Valmoriany was to be a jewel in the crown of the Armaralo Initiativea thriving urban center perched on steep slopes, with cable cars climbing sheer cliffs, luxury lodges, and ski runs winding through pristine snowfields.

From the outset, engineers and planners faced formidable obstacles.
The fault line beneath the mountains was an ever-present threata geological scar that could awaken with devastating earthquakes or avalanches. The steep terrain complicated construction logistics, with narrow roads and precarious drop-offs challenging supply convoys.
Local Armaralan experts warned of the mountains instability, but the pressure from Wessernias government to deliver progress quickly meant some warnings were downplayed.

Heavy machinery carved terraces into the mountainside, blasting rock and moving earth to create foundations for roads, hotels, and recreational facilities.
Teams of workers labored in harsh winter conditions, facing bitter cold and treacherous footing. Engineers installed early-warning systems and monitored seismic activity, but natures unpredictability remained a wild card.

One bleak morning in late winter, the warning sirens blared too late.
A massive avalanche thundered down the eastern slope of the Pantgruel range, triggered by the destabilization of snowpack from recent construction blasting.
Tons of snow, ice, and debris buried a remote work camp and parts of the access road.
Rescue teams scrambled through freezing conditions, but the toll was graveseventeen workers lost their lives, dozens injured, and equipment destroyed.

News of the disaster shocked both New Valmoriany and Wessernia. The tragedy forced a halt to construction as investigations began.
Head Council Mack Messiaon expressed deep condolences and vowed to strengthen safety protocols.
The incident ignited fierce debate within the Council. Some argued for scaling back the project to prioritize safety and environmental stewardship. Others, driven by urgency, pushed to continue with renewed caution.

Among those affected was Amira Selen, a young project manager who had overseen parts of the resorts infrastructure. She wrestled with guilt and grief but remained committed to honoring the victims by building a city that could coexist with the mountains harsh realities.
Meanwhile, local Armaralan environmentalists called for greater respect for the land, warning that New Valmorianys location on a fault line was a dangerous gamble.

The avalanche was a harsh reminder that progress on Armaralo came with risksboth human and natural. New Valmorianys future would depend on balancing ambition with humility and forging new paths in engineering, safety, and community cooperation.

(Heres a story from one person present during and after the avalanche) Amira Selen wiped the streaks of dirt and snow from her face, her breath visible in the frigid mountain air. She stood on a ridge overlooking New Valmorianys construction zone, now eerily quiet after the avalanche that had taken so many lives.
As the projects young but driven infrastructure manager, Amira had been proud of her role in turning this ambitious vision into reality. She had overseen everything from road networks to energy grids, pushing against the mountains challenges with determination.
But the disaster changed everything.

For days, she had barely slept, haunted by memories of the rescue efforts and faces of those lost. Survivors told harrowing tales of snow and rock swallowing their camps, the frantic scramble to safety, and the piercing cold that tested every ounce of human endurance.
Amira poured over safety reports and geological data, searching for what had gone wrong. Was it an unpredictable natural event, or had human error pushed the fragile mountain beyond its limits?
Her team worked tirelessly with investigators, combing through evidenceexamining blast sites, interviewing workers, and analyzing snowpack conditions.

At night, Amira wrote letters to the families of the victims, struggling to find the words that could express the sorrow and responsibility she felt. The weight of leadership pressed heavily on her shoulders.
Back in Wessernia, the Council of Thirteen convened in an emergency session. The chamber was thick with tension.
Councilor Varrin Kehl slammed his fist on the table. This tragedy was preventable! We ignored warnings and rushed headlong into a disaster zone. Its time to rethink the entire New Valmoriany project.
Councilor Mara Den argued passionately. We must not let fear paralyze us. This city represents hope, growth, and survival. We owe it to the workers and the nation to continue  but with tighter safety and environmental protocols.
Head Council Mack Messiaon listened carefully. Both points are valid. We face a difficult balance  ambition and caution. We owe respect to those lost and must learn from this.
Councilor Reva Dorn proposed merging all of its investigation bureaus into one investigation bureau that would be known as the Western View Complete Investigation Bureau or WVCIB to investigate the avalanche and review safety standards before any further construction.
The WVCIB, led by John Gartidued, began a thorough inquiry.
They analyzed seismic records, weather data, and construction logs. The investigation revealed a combination of factors:

Recent blasting had weakened critical snowpack layers.

Unseasonably heavy snowfall increased avalanche risk.

Early warning systems were functional but response protocols were insufficiently rehearsed.

Communication breakdowns delayed evacuation efforts.

The report recommended:

Immediate suspension of high-risk construction during heavy snow seasons.

Enhanced training and drills for emergency response.

Investment in advanced monitoring technology for real-time avalanche prediction.

Greater involvement of local Armaralan experts familiar with the mountains behavior.

John Gartidued presented the findings to the Council, with Amira Selen accepting full responsibility for oversights while pledging to implement all recommended changes.

The tragedy of New Valmoriany became a catalyst for reformreminding Western View that progress on Armaralo required humility, respect for nature, and the lives of those building the future. But it wasnt just New Valmoriany that was hit by the humungous avalanche.
